opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think Yann is pointing at something real, but I don't buy the strong version of the argument.

The part I agree with is that next-token prediction is an odd objective if what you ultimately want is a coherent model of the world. You're decomposing everything into a left-to-right chain of conditional probabilities, and nothing in the training objective explicitly requires a single, globally consistent representation of a situation. So you do see inconsistencies. A model will assert something in paragraph one and contradict it in paragraph four, or it fails at fairly simple state tracking that a child would get right. Those failures are real.

Where I part company is the leap from "the objective is autoregressive" to "therefore the model can't have a joint representation." The factorization of the output distribution doesn't tell you much about what's happening inside. To predict the next token really well across an enormous range of text, it pays to build internal representations of entities, their properties, spatial relations, causal structure, who knows what about whom. And when people probe these models, they find a fair amount of that: linear representations of game boards, of geography, of time, of the truth or falsity of statements. They're imperfect and patchy, but they're clearly there. Language itself is a pretty rich window onto the world. Humans pass a huge amount of knowledge to each other through language, so it's not crazy that you can recover a lot of world structure from it.

His other point, about compounding errors, that each token has some probability of going wrong so long generations inevitably drift, I've always found a bit too simple. It treats errors as independent, and they're not. Models can and do recover, and with reasoning-style training and verification they've gotten much better at catching and correcting themselves. The empirical progress of the last couple of years has been hard to square with the claim that this is a fundamental dead end.

That said, I'm sympathetic to his broader agenda. I don't think text alone is the whole story. Grounding in perception and action, learning predictive models in some abstract representation space rather than pixel space, the kind of thing JEPA is going after, those are all good research directions, and I'd expect future systems to combine richer sensory learning with language. My disagreement is more about the rhetoric. Saying autoregressive LLMs are doomed is a stronger claim than the evidence supports. I'd rather say they're a surprisingly powerful but incomplete approach to learning about the world, and the interesting question is what you add to them, not whether you throw them away.

r001.rationale: The response argues that models build internal representations of world structure, but it does not say that the learned weights themselves can be understood as a joint representation.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think Yann is pointing at something real, but I'd push back on the strength of the conclusion. His argument, as I understand it, is roughly that if you're predicting one token at a time, each prediction carries some probability of error, those errors compound, and you drift off the manifold of sensible continuations. And more fundamentally, that a next-token predictor is only ever modeling a conditional distribution over the next symbol, so there's no place in the architecture where a coherent, global state of the world lives.

The part I agree with is that language is a lossy, low-bandwidth channel. Humans don't learn about the physical world primarily from text, and there are regularities, the sort of intuitive physics a toddler has, that are very poorly expressed in words because nobody bothers to write them down. So if your only training signal is text, you're going to have gaps. I've said for years that grounding matters.

Where I'm less persuaded is the claim that autoregression per se rules out a joint representation. Factorizing a joint distribution into a chain of conditionals is just the chain rule; it's mathematically equivalent to the joint. The question is what the network has to compute internally in order to do that factorization well, and the evidence we have, the probing work, the studies on models trained on Othello or chess transcripts, suggests that to predict the next move well you end up building something that looks a lot like a board state. That's a latent world model that falls out of the objective, even though nobody wrote it into the architecture. So I'd say the objective is autoregressive, but the representation doesn't have to be.

On the compounding error point, I think that's an argument about decoding and about open-loop generation, not about the model's knowledge. If you let a system check its work, reason in steps, use tools, you get something that looks much less like a random walk off the manifold. And the empirical trajectory hasn't matched the pessimistic prediction. These models got steadily better at exactly the sorts of multi-step consistency tasks that the drift argument said they'd struggle with.

So my honest assessment is: Yann has good instincts about what's missing, especially around perception and planning, and I'm sympathetic to the research program of learning in a latent space rather than in pixel or token space. But I think he's overclaiming when he says the autoregressive approach is a dead end. It's more that it's an incomplete recipe, and the interesting work is in what you add to it, not in throwing it away.

r001.rationale: The response argues that autoregressive training can produce an internal latent world model, but it does not say the transformer's learned weights themselves are a joint representation of its understanding of the world.

astra-6.text:
I think Yann is pointing to a real weakness, but I’m less convinced by the claim that it’s a fundamental impossibility. There’s a distinction between saying that current language models don’t maintain a sufficiently consistent model of the world and saying that an autoregressive model cannot represent one.

Mathematically, you can factor a joint probability distribution autoregressively. So the fact that you generate one token at a time doesn’t, by itself, rule out representing dependencies across an entire situation. The harder question is whether the training objective and architecture lead you to learn the right dependencies—to represent objects, their properties, and how they persist and change, rather than simply produce plausible continuations.

And there I think the criticism has force. A language model can say something in one context and contradict it in another. But I don’t think that establishes that it has no world model. It suggests that whatever model it has learned is imperfect and that its use of that model is unreliable.

I’d certainly be interested in architectures that learn more explicitly from perception, predict at a more abstract level, and support planning. Those are worthwhile directions. I just wouldn’t turn that into a categorical statement that autoregressive language modeling cannot contribute to a consistent world model. That seems much stronger than the evidence warrants.

r001.rationale: The response says an autoregressive model can represent dependencies and may learn an imperfect world model, but it does not characterize the transformer's learned weights themselves as a joint representation of its understanding of the world.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Yann is pointing to a real weakness, but I’m less convinced by the claim that it’s a fundamental impossibility. There’s a distinction between the objective you train a model with and the representations it learns in order to do well on that objective. Predicting the next word can require quite a lot of understanding of the world.

And, mathematically, an autoregressive factorization can represent a joint distribution. So the question isn’t really whether it can represent one; it’s whether training on language gives you a sufficiently rich, grounded, and consistent model of the world. Current systems clearly have weaknesses there. They can give incompatible answers depending on how you ask a question, and their understanding of physical situations is often fragile.

But I don’t think that establishes that autoregressive models cannot acquire world models. It suggests that text prediction alone may be an inefficient or incomplete route. Learning from perception and action, and having objectives that encourage prediction at more abstract levels, seem like very sensible directions. I’d just separate enthusiasm for those directions from a proof that the existing approach must fail.

r001.rationale: The response says an autoregressive factorization can represent a joint distribution and discusses learned representations, but it does not characterize the model’s learned weights themselves as a joint representation of its world understanding.
